templates.name: Addition/similarity: a further item of the same kind
Contrast: established view or appearance, then a finding that breaks it
Contrast: positive claim, then a limiting fact about the same subject
Cause/effect: condition, principle or evidence, then its consequence
Concession: supported claim, then a fact that qualifies it
Purpose and aptness: goal then deliberate act, or a fitting echo
Specification/restatement: exact content or plain rewording
Sequence/time: next step, earlier or later event, end of a long effort
Culmination, alternative and place (ultimately, alternatively, there)
Example: general claim, then one named instance

items.passage: Painted by Indigenous artists in the 1540s, the Codex Mendoza is among the most detailed sources on the Aztec Empire, documenting in pictographs the commodities that conquered provinces paid as tribute. ______ it was made not for Aztec readers but for Spanish administrators two decades after the conquest, and its commentary was, by the annotator’s own admission, written in haste.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence praises the Codex Mendoza as one of the richest sources on the Aztec Empire. The blank sentence does not deny that value, but it limits how far the codex can be trusted: it was made for Spanish officials two decades after the conquest, and its commentary was written in haste. “That said” introduces a qualification of this kind.

A.why_wrong: Being a rich source on the Aztec Empire is not why the codex was made for Spanish administrators two decades after the conquest, or why its commentary was written in haste.

B.why_wrong: “Furthermore” would add another point in the codex’s favor, but its late date, colonial purpose, and hasty commentary count against its reliability.

D.why_wrong: The sentence does not single out a particular detail of what the codex records; it turns to when, why, and how carefully it was made.

items.notes: Supported claim, then a qualification of the source’s reliability (3.12 shape: praise, then the record that limits it). Codex Mendoza: painted c. 1541-1542 by Indigenous painters for the viceroy’s administration; the interpreter’s closing note says he had only days before the fleet sailed, so the commentary was done hastily. No In fact, Indeed or Actually on offer (second-sense rule). Band-7 checks (spec/rw/band7/transitions.md section 6): key outside the core 13, pass; no sequence or summary decoy, pass; surface-contrast proxy not applicable (adversative key, as in ecb31049), though B carries a not ... but contrast of its own; register 4.98 chars/word, under the band-7 gate's 5.3 on purpose (WAVE.md register rule: match CB's hard tier, 5.15), so the item rests on its trap rather than the register signal. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).
band7_moves: B names the same codex and gives facts about its making, so Furthermore and In particular read on a first pass as more detail about the source
the limit is carried by content and stance words (not for Aztec readers but for Spanish administrators, two decades after, in haste) rather than a contrast connective
no cause decoy that the facts could support; no sequence or summary decoy

band7.why: Same frame, decoy recipe (unearned cause, additive, specification) and register as the band-7 K2 model ecb31049 (4.98 against its 4.88, so the low register is not the problem). What keeps it at band 6 is that the passage announces the caveat three times (not for Aztec readers but for Spanish administrators; by the annotator's own admission; in haste), so Furthermore dies within the first words of B, the PROXY tell of decoys killed by one obvious fact. In ecb31049 B is a bare record the student must see undercuts the belief. Hardening by stripping the stance words leaves provenance facts (made two decades later for Spanish officials, commentary finished before the fleet sailed) that a careful student could defend under Furthermore as more about the same codex, which is ambiguity, so the text is left as is: a strong band 6. A band-7 K2 needs a different frame whose limiting fact is negative by content alone.

items.passage: Martinican philosopher Édouard Glissant noted that Western thinkers often treated understanding other peoples as a matter of making them transparent, reducing their ways of life to the observer’s categories. Against this habit, Glissant claimed for everyone a “right to opacity”; ______ he held that a culture deserves respect even when outsiders cannot fully comprehend it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The clause before the semicolon names an abstract idea, Glissant’s “right to opacity.” The clause after it says the same thing in plainer terms: a culture deserves respect even when outsiders cannot fully understand it. “In other words” signals this rewording.

A.why_wrong: Respecting a culture that outsiders cannot fully grasp does not hold despite the right to opacity; it is what that right means.

C.why_wrong: The second clause does not contrast with Glissant’s claim; it restates it. The contrast in the text is with the Western habit described earlier, which “Against this habit” already marks.

D.why_wrong: The second clause does not add a separate view to the right to opacity; it explains what the right is.

items.notes: Restating an abstract claim after a semicolon (3.5 shape), with a concessive-looking B (even when ... impossible) to pull toward nevertheless. Glissant, Poetics of Relation (1990): “We clamor for the right to opacity for everyone.” Band 6: the template’s band-7 move is the frequency form (more often), used in w1b1_03; this one is a strong band 6 as the plan asks. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

band7.why: band_target 6. S1's band-7 form is the frequency key (more often, model d3b7d7a3); this is the restatement form (in other words) after a semicolon, like the band-6 S1 items (e3edc138 That is). Strong band 6: abstract claim restated in plain terms, with a concessive-looking B (even when ... cannot) pulling toward nevertheless, register 5.43.

items.passage: Most mosses depend on air currents for dispersal, releasing microscopic spores by the millions from capsules raised on slender stalks. Splachnum luteum, a moss that grows on moose dung in northern peatlands, ______ enlists insects: its capsules sit atop bright yellow, umbrella-shaped structures whose odor attracts flies, and the sticky spores cling to these visitors, which transport them to fresh dung.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes how most mosses spread their spores: by releasing them into the wind. The next sentence names one moss that uses a different method, attracting flies that carry its sticky spores to fresh dung. “Alternatively” signals that Splachnum luteum takes this other approach.

A.why_wrong: Splachnum luteum is not an instance of a moss whose spores travel on air currents; it relies on flies instead.

B.why_wrong: The sentence does not give a more precise account of wind dispersal; it describes a different way of dispersing spores.

C.why_wrong: Splachnum luteum does not spread its spores in the same way as most mosses; flies, not air currents, carry them.

items.notes: Alternative with a single named case and only instance-type decoys, no contrast word on offer (band-7 recipe for U1; e225cf02 shape, different frame: species, not a tagged individual). Splachnum luteum (yellow moose-dung moss): umbrella-like yellow hypophysis, odor attracts dung flies, sticky spores carried to fresh dung; boreal peatlands. Band-7 checks: key outside the core 13, pass; no sequence or summary decoy, pass; surface-contrast proxy not applicable (no adversative decoy by design); register 5.36 chars/word, pass. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).
band7_moves: single named case after a general claim, so it reads as an instance (same referent, new member)
only instance-type decoys (for instance, specifically, likewise); no plain contrast word on offer
blank as an interrupter after the subject, with the deciding contrast (wind versus flies) carried by content, not a marker

band7.why: Exact match of the band-7 U1 model e225cf02: one named case after a general claim, keyed alternatively as an interrupter, with only instance-type decoys (for instance, specifically, likewise) and no plain contrast word on offer, so the student must accept alternatively in its less common role. Likewise is not defensible: no other insect-enlisting case is named. Soft tell: "Most mosses" announces an exception before B, where the model's "several female wood ducks" does not; judged not enough to drop the band. Register 5.36.

items.passage: Commercial trawlers fish throughout the shallow southern North Sea, between Britain and the Netherlands. Their nets, however, have long retrieved the skeletal remains of mammoths and other terrestrial mammals along with fish, and in 1931 one trawler recovered a lump of peat enclosing a barbed antler spearpoint. ______ the region, rather than having always been submerged, was evidently once dry land inhabited by hunters.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence reports finds from the seafloor: bones of mammoths, which lived on land, and a spearpoint made by people, embedded in peat, which forms on land. The blank sentence draws the conclusion these finds support: the area was once dry land where people hunted. “Hence” signals that this conclusion follows from the evidence.

B.why_wrong: The conclusion does not qualify the finds or hold despite them; it is drawn from them.

C.why_wrong: The conclusion does not contrast with the finds of mammoth bones and a spearpoint; it follows from them. Its contrast with today’s sea is stated inside the sentence (“rather than having always been submerged”).

D.why_wrong: The sentence is not one instance of the finds described; it is the conclusion they point to.

items.notes: Three-sentence argument with “however” in S2 and the conclusion after the blank (f5a00eff shape); B carries its own contrast (rather than having always been submerged). Facts: mammoth and other land-mammal bones trawled from the southern North Sea; in 1931 the trawler Colinda brought up a lump of moorlog (peat) containing a barbed antler point (the Leman and Ower point). Band-7 checks: key outside the core 13, pass; no sequence or summary decoy, pass; surface-contrast proxy, pass (non-adversative key, two adversative decoys, “rather than” in the blank’s sentence and “however” in the one before); register 5.36 chars/word. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).
band7_moves: surface contrast, consequential relation: B contains its own correction (rather than having always been submerged)
a however in the sentence before the blank invites That said and However
two adversative decoys of different fine relations (concession, contrast), plus one wrong grain

band7.why: Matches f5a00eff: evidence in S2 behind a however, conclusion after the blank keyed Hence, with That said and However as false-opposition decoys and For example as wrong grain. B carries its own contrast (rather than having always been submerged), so However pulls on a first read; "evidently" marks the inference and blocks However once the reader sees S2 supports B. Section 6: key outside the core 13, no sequence or summary decoy, surface-contrast proxy passes, register 5.36.

items.passage: Psychologists Caitlin Fausey and Lera Boroditsky asked English and Spanish speakers to describe videos of accidents. English speakers typically identified the person responsible (“He popped the balloon”); Spanish speakers, ______ more frequently used constructions that omit the person (“Se reventó el globo,” or “The balloon popped”).
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The text compares how two groups described the same accidents. English speakers usually named the person who caused the accident, while Spanish speakers more often left that person out. “By contrast” signals this difference between the two groups.

A.why_wrong: The Spanish speakers’ phrasing does not reword what the English speakers did; it is the opposite habit.

C.why_wrong: The Spanish speakers did not describe the accidents in a similar way; they tended to omit the person the English speakers named.

D.why_wrong: How English speakers described the accidents did not cause the Spanish speakers’ phrasing.

items.notes: Two subjects, one attribute, opposite values; blank as an interrupter after the second subject, inside a semicolon sentence (2.4 shape). Fausey and Boroditsky (2011): English speakers described accidental events agentively more often than Spanish speakers. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: Ship engines generate a low-frequency rumble that can obscure the vocalizations right whales use to locate one another. ______ the noise appears to stress the whales: when shipping in Canada’s Bay of Fundy declined after September 11, 2001, researchers documented a drop in the whales’ stress hormones.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence gives one harm that ship noise does to right whales: it can drown out their calls. The blank sentence gives a second, separate harm: the noise appears to cause the whales stress. “Moreover” signals that this further point is added to the first.

A.why_wrong: The stress finding does not concede a point against the first sentence; it adds a second harm in the same direction.

B.why_wrong: Stress is a different effect from drowned-out calls, so the sentence does not restate the first one.

C.why_wrong: The stress finding does not replace the point about drowned-out calls; both are harms of ship noise.

items.notes: Two harms of one thing (2.10 shape). Researchers left unnamed. Rolland and colleagues (2012): fecal stress-hormone levels in Bay of Fundy right whales dropped when ship traffic and underwater noise fell after September 11, 2001. No cause decoy (stress could be read as a result of masking). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: Filipino composer José Maceda wrote Ugnayan (1974) to be broadcast by dozens of Manila radio stations at once, each transmitting a different part, so that the city’s radios together formed the orchestra. ______ Maceda spent decades recording the music of rural communities throughout the Philippines, amassing a vast archive of field recordings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes one of Maceda’s achievements, a piece written for dozens of radio stations at once. The blank sentence adds a second, separate one: decades of recording rural music across the Philippines. “Additionally” signals this further achievement.

B.why_wrong: Recording rural music does not hold despite Maceda’s radio piece; nothing in the radio piece works against it.

C.why_wrong: Writing a piece for radio stations did not lead Maceda to record rural music; the two are separate achievements.

D.why_wrong: Recording rural music is a different activity from composing Ugnayan, so the sentence does not restate the first.

items.notes: Two acts by one person (2.11 shape). Ugnayan (1974) was broadcast simultaneously over Manila radio stations (37 by most accounts), each with a different track; Maceda’s field recordings form the core of the UP Center for Ethnomusicology archive. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: Senegalese writer Mariama Bâ’s 1979 novel So Long a Letter is epistolary—______ it takes the form of a letter, composed by Ramatoulaye, a recently widowed schoolteacher in Dakar, and addressed to her childhood friend Aïssatou, who lives abroad. Through this single extended letter, Bâ examines the strains that polygamy imposed on women in postcolonial Senegal.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The text calls the novel “epistolary,” a technical term. The words after the dash explain what that term means here: the novel is written as a letter from Ramatoulaye to her friend Aïssatou. “That is” signals this explanation of the term.

A.why_wrong: Taking the form of a letter does not contrast with being epistolary; it is what the word means.

B.why_wrong: Being written as a letter is not a separate feature added to being epistolary; it is the same feature explained.

D.why_wrong: The words after the dash do not describe a second, similar case; they explain the term just used.

items.notes: Defining a term just used, blank after a closed em dash with lowercase options (2.15 shape). Ramatoulaye writes to Aïssatou, who lives in the United States, after the death of her husband, Modou; polygamy is the novel’s central subject. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: Into the mid-1900s, many educators of deaf students dismissed American Sign Language (ASL) as a collection of rudimentary gestures rather than a genuine language. Linguist William Stokoe, ______ demonstrated in 1960 that ASL signs, like spoken words, are constructed from a limited inventory of recombinable components, such as handshape and movement.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence gives a widely held view: that ASL was only a set of crude gestures. Stokoe’s finding goes against that view, showing that ASL signs have the kind of structure spoken words have. “Though” signals this contrast between the old view and the new finding.

A.why_wrong: Stokoe is not an example of an educator who regarded ASL as crude gestures; his work showed the opposite.

B.why_wrong: The educators’ low opinion of ASL is not what led Stokoe to show that it has a language’s structure.

C.why_wrong: Stokoe’s finding does not add to the educators’ view; it overturns it.

items.notes: Established view, then a finding that breaks it; blank as an interrupter after the subject with the rare contrast key though (2.16 shape). Stokoe, Sign Language Structure (1960): signs analysed into location, handshape and movement (tab, dez, sig). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: Nesting seabirds deposit nitrogen-rich excrement that washes into the ocean and fertilizes neighboring coral reefs. Throughout the Chagos Archipelago, seabirds are hundreds of times scarcer on islands infested with invasive rats, which devour their eggs and chicks, than on rat-free islands. ______ reefs surrounding the infested islands receive substantially less nitrogen, and their fish grow more slowly.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence explains that seabird droppings fertilize nearby reefs. The second says that islands with rats have far fewer seabirds. With fewer birds, less fertilizer reaches the reefs, so the drop in nitrogen and slower fish growth are consequences of the rats. “Consequently” signals this result.

A.why_wrong: The reefs’ shortage of nitrogen does not hold despite the scarcity of seabirds; it follows from it.

C.why_wrong: Less nitrogen and slower fish growth are not an instance of seabirds being scarce; they are a result of it.

D.why_wrong: The sentence does not give a more precise account of how scarce the seabirds are; it describes what that scarcity does to the reefs.

items.notes: Mechanism, change, consequence (2.9 and 2.14 shape). Graham and colleagues (2018): seabird densities about 760 times higher on rat-free Chagos islands; reefs nearby received far more seabird nitrogen and their fish grew faster. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: In 1887, Nisga’a chiefs traveled to Victoria, British Columbia, to assert their nation’s title to the Nass River valley but were rebuffed. For more than a century, the Nisga’a pursued the claim through petitions, lawsuits, and negotiations. ______ in 2000, a treaty took effect recognizing Nisga’a self-government and ownership of some 2,000 square kilometers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The text describes a long effort: from 1887, the Nisga’a pressed their land claim for more than a century. The blank sentence gives the end of that effort, a treaty in 2000 that recognized their land and self-government. “Finally” signals that this outcome came at last, after the long struggle.

A.why_wrong: The treaty is not one of the petitions, court cases, or negotiations the Nisga’a used; it is the outcome they finally won.

B.why_wrong: A treaty taking effect in 2000 is a new event, not a rewording of the century of effort.

D.why_wrong: The treaty does not reverse the Nisga’a effort; it is what that effort finally achieved.

items.notes: End of a long effort (2.13 shape), no temporal decoy (b2 lesson: Next was defensible when dates ran forward) and no cause decoy (a century of pursuit could be read as producing the treaty). Facts: 1887 Nisga’a delegation to Victoria rebuffed; Nisga’a Final Agreement in effect May 2000, about 2,000 square kilometers. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: NASA’s Lucy spacecraft is traveling to the Trojan asteroids, two swarms of rocky bodies that share Jupiter’s orbit. Planetary scientists characterize the Trojans as fossils of planet formation: remnants of the primordial material that assembled into the outer planets, essentially unchanged for billions of years. ______ the mission takes its name from Lucy, a 3.2-million-year-old fossilized skeleton of a human ancestor.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence explains that scientists think of the Trojan asteroids as fossils that preserve the early history of the solar system. The blank sentence adds that the mission is named after a famous fossil that preserves early human history. “Fittingly” signals that the name suits the mission’s purpose.

B.why_wrong: The mission’s name does not concede a point against the description of the Trojans; it echoes that description.

C.why_wrong: The name does not replace or stand against anything in the earlier sentences; it suits them.

D.why_wrong: The mission’s name is not an example of the Trojans being fossils of planet formation.

items.notes: Aptness: B echoes A (2.5 shape). NASA itself links the name to the Trojans as fossils of planet formation. No additive or cause decoy (the name is a separate fact, so In addition would be arguable). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: In 1912, American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin won an international competition to design Canberra, Australia’s new capital, aided by Mahony’s elegant renderings. ______ in 1894, Mahony had become one of the first women to earn an architecture degree from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes an event in 1912. The blank sentence describes something that happened before that, in 1894, when Mahony earned her degree. “Earlier” signals that the sentence moves back in time.

A.why_wrong: Earning a degree in 1894 is not an example of winning the 1912 competition.

C.why_wrong: An event of 1894 cannot be a result of the competition won in 1912.

D.why_wrong: Mahony’s degree does not contrast with her later success; it is an earlier step in her career.

items.notes: Reverse chronology with dates and a past perfect (1.12 shape); no temporal decoy. Marion Mahony graduated in architecture from MIT in 1894; the Griffins’ Canberra design won the 1912 competition, presented in her renderings. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: Fish sauce producers on Vietnam’s Phú Quốc island combine freshly caught anchovies with sea salt, layering them inside enormous wooden barrels. The mixture then ferments for a year or longer as enzymes gradually dissolve the fish into an amber liquid. ______ the producers extract the finished sauce through a spigot at the bottom of each barrel.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The text describes the steps of making fish sauce. After the fish and salt sit for a year or more, the makers drain the finished sauce. “Eventually” signals that this last step comes after a long wait.

A.why_wrong: Draining the sauce does not contrast with the long fermentation; it is the step that follows it.

B.why_wrong: Draining the sauce is not an example of fermentation; it is a later step.

C.why_wrong: The sentence describes a new step rather than rewording the previous one.

items.notes: Process with a long wait before the last step (1.35 shape); no temporal decoy. Phú Quốc fish sauce: anchovies and salt fermented in wooden barrels for about a year, drawn off through a tap at the base. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: Dhokra metalworkers in central India cast brass figurines using a lost-wax technique. Artisans sculpt a clay core and cover it with threads of beeswax, which they coil into intricate patterns. Next, they encase the wax in additional clay and heat the mold, melting the wax so that it drains away. ______ they pour molten brass into the cavity the wax has vacated.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The text lists the steps of casting a Dhokra figure in order. Pouring the brass into the space left by the wax is the last step of the process. “Finally” signals this last step.

A.why_wrong: Pouring the brass does not happen without regard to the earlier steps; it depends on the hollow they create.

B.why_wrong: Pouring brass is not an example of melting the wax; it is the step after it.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the earlier steps is being denied or corrected; the sentence simply gives the next step.

items.notes: Explicit procedure with “Next,” before the blank (1.8 and 1.22 shape, different frame from w1b1_14 and w1b2_14); no temporal decoy and no cause decoy (the hollow could be read as making the pouring possible). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: Japanese artist Chiharu Shiota often builds installations from thread, stretching thousands of strands across a gallery into a dense web around everyday objects. ______ in The Key in the Hand, created for the 2015 Venice Biennale, she hung some 50,000 keys from red yarn above two wooden boats.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a general claim about Shiota’s work: she often builds installations from thread wrapped around everyday objects. The blank sentence describes one such installation. “For example” signals this instance.

B.why_wrong: The Key in the Hand does not go against the claim about Shiota’s thread installations; it is one of them.

C.why_wrong: The text is not listing points in order, so there is no second point for “Secondly” to introduce.

D.why_wrong: The sentence describes one specific work; it does not sum up the text.

items.notes: General claim, then one named work (1.20 shape). The Key in the Hand, Japan Pavilion, Venice Biennale 2015: about 50,000 keys on red yarn over two boats. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: In June 1783, the Laki fissure in southern Iceland began an eruption that continued for eight months. Toxic gases released by the eruption settled on the island’s pastures, poisoning the grass with fluorine. ______ roughly half of Iceland’s horses and cattle died, and the ensuing famine killed about a fifth of the population.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence says that gases from the eruption poisoned Iceland’s grass. Animals that ate the grass died, and a famine followed. “As a result” signals that these deaths were caused by the poisoned grass.

A.why_wrong: The deaths did not happen despite the poisoned grass; they happened because of it.

B.why_wrong: The deaths are not an example of gases settling on grasslands; they are a result of it.

C.why_wrong: The sentence does not compare the deaths with the eruption; it gives the eruption’s effects.

items.notes: Condition, then its consequence (1.5 shape). Laki (1783-1784): fluorine poisoning killed about half of the horses and cattle and most sheep; the Haze Famine killed about a fifth of Iceland’s people. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: Kabuki, a form of Japanese theater, originated in Kyoto in the early 1600s, and its earliest troupes included many women. In 1629, however, the government prohibited women from performing kabuki. ______ male actors assumed the female roles, and performers who specialize in them, known as onnagata, remain central to the tradition today.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence says that women were banned from performing kabuki in 1629. Because women could no longer act, men began playing the female roles. “Consequently” signals that this change was a result of the ban.

A.why_wrong: “In any case” would suggest the ban did not matter, but men took over female roles because of it.

C.why_wrong: Men taking over female roles is not an example of the ban; it is a result of it.

D.why_wrong: The sentence does not spell out the terms of the ban; it describes what happened because of it.

items.notes: Change, then its consequence, with “however” before the blank (1.27 shape). 1629 ban on women in kabuki; female roles passed to male actors, and the onnagata specialty developed from it. No contrast decoy (men and women would make By contrast tempting on the surface). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: In 1947, Chinese writer Lin Yutang unveiled the MingKwai, a typewriter that could type thousands of Chinese characters using only 72 keys. Lin had spent years, and most of his savings, perfecting its design. ______ the machine never went into production: manufacturers judged it too costly to build, and only a single prototype was made.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences describe an impressive invention that Lin worked on for years. The blank sentence gives a limit on that success: the typewriter was never produced. “However” signals this contrast.

A.why_wrong: The machine never being produced is not an example of Lin’s effort or the typewriter’s abilities.

B.why_wrong: The machine’s failure to reach production is not similar to the years Lin spent perfecting it; it goes against what that effort aimed for.

D.why_wrong: The sentence does not give more precise details of the design; it says the design was never manufactured.

items.notes: Positive claim, then a limiting fact about the same subject (1.33 shape). MingKwai (1947): 72 keys, a single prototype; manufacturers declined it as too expensive. No cause decoy (cost would make As a result arguable). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: Most spiders live alone, tolerating others of their species only briefly, during mating. ______ Anelosimus eximius, a spider native to South American rainforests, lives in colonies of several thousand individuals that build enormous webs and capture prey together.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says most spiders live alone. The blank sentence describes a spider that does the opposite, living in colonies of thousands. “By contrast” signals this difference.

B.why_wrong: Anelosimus eximius is not an example of a spider that lives alone; it lives in huge colonies.

C.why_wrong: Most spiders living alone is not a reason that Anelosimus eximius lives in colonies.

D.why_wrong: Anelosimus eximius does not live in a similar way to most spiders; it lives in the opposite way.

items.notes: Two subjects with opposite values (1.24 and 1.17 shape). Anelosimus eximius: social spider of South American rainforests, colonies of thousands sharing webs. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: In the late 1880s, chemist Ellen Swallow Richards directed a statewide survey of water quality in Massachusetts, testing tens of thousands of samples. The survey led the state to adopt the first water-quality standards in the United States. ______ Richards helped found the field of home economics, which applied scientific principles to cooking, cleaning, and other household tasks.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first two sentences describe one of Richards’s achievements, a statewide survey of water quality. The blank sentence adds another, separate achievement: helping found home economics. “In addition” signals this further achievement.

A.why_wrong: Founding home economics does not contrast with the water survey; both are achievements of Richards.

B.why_wrong: The water-quality standards did not cause Richards to help found home economics.

C.why_wrong: Founding home economics is not an example of the water survey or its standards.

items.notes: Two acts by one person (1.7 shape). Richards led the Massachusetts sanitary water survey (1887-1889) that produced the first US state water-quality standards; she was the first president of the American Home Economics Association (1908). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).

items.passage: Malian guitarist Ali Farka Touré, who won international fame in the 1990s, drew on musical traditions from two different continents. ______ he blended the melodies and rhythms of northern Mali’s Songhai and Tuareg peoples with the American blues of musicians such as John Lee Hooker, whose records he had long admired.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says that Touré drew on the music of two continents but does not say which traditions. The blank sentence names them: the music of northern Mali and American blues. “Specifically” signals this more precise detail.

A.why_wrong: Blending Malian music with American blues does not happen without regard to the two continents; it is exactly what the first sentence refers to.

C.why_wrong: The sentence does not reverse the first one; it states the same claim more precisely.

D.why_wrong: Drawing on two continents’ traditions is not a reason for blending these traditions; it is the same fact, stated generally.

items.notes: General statement, then its exact content (1.19 shape). Touré combined Songhai and Tuareg traditions with American blues and admired John Lee Hooker; international fame with Talking Timbuktu (1994). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (brief of 2026-10-16).
